Submission: 10/29/2026 RadioLink Team Website

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: • This datasheet documents the design of my individual subsystem for the Team 105 embedded systems project, from block diagram and component selection through schematic, power budget, PCB, and testing. It records the engineering decisions behind my portion of the system so it can be understood, reproduced, and evaluated.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
• Team 105 is developing RadioLink, a portable, off-grid communication device for when cellular or internet service is unavailable. Each team member builds one subsystem around a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, and the boards connect through standardized connectors with a shared ground.
  • My subsystem is audio input. A CMC-6027-24T electret microphone captures the user’s voice, and an MCP6004 amplifier stage boosts the signal for the PIC’s analog-to-digital converter. The board runs from a single 3.3 V supply.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
• I am responsible for the microphone subsystem: selecting the components, designing the amplifier circuit, and creating the schematic, PCB, power budget, and test features. The board includes a UART header, a pushbutton, and a test LED to support debugging.
  • The following sections cover the block diagram, component selection, bill of materials, schematic, power budget, PCB design, and verification results.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Microphone Input Block Diagram - Power starts at a 9 volt DC wall adapter (unregulated), which plugs into the barrel jack and feeds the 5V Voltage Regulator LM7805. The regulator's 5 volt output powers the Curiosity Nano through its VTG pin, along with the microphone and the op amp. The signal starts at a CUI Devices electret microphone. It’s small and cheap, but its output is only millivolts, so it goes into an MCP6004 op amp. I chose that op amp because it’s rail-to-rail, runs from 5 volts, and has four amplifiers in one chip, so I use one and have spares. The amplified signal goes to pin RA0, the ADC on the PIC18F57Q43, which turns sound into numbers. I send those numbers out over UART. I chose UART because it needs only TX, RX and ground, it’s built into the Curiosity Nano, and it connects straight to Sultan’s board through connector 1. I also have a push button on RC4 and a test LED on RC5, which the PIC drives.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Table 1: DAC Component Selection

Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) — Individual Subsystem

Solution Pros Cons * Option 1. * PIC18F57Q43 Internal 8-bit DAC* No additional cost* Link to product * No additional cost* 8-bit output enough for speech* No SPI communication required * Only 8-bit resolution* Limited processing horsepower for DSP* RAM constraints for audio buffering * Option 2. * Texas Instruments DAC7512 * $7/each * Link to product * Excellent audio fidelity (12-bit resolution)* Rapid serial communication (up to 30 MHz)* Glitch-free power-on initialization * More expensive* No breadboard-friendly DIP package* Requires a completely custom software driver * Option 3. * Microchip MCP4725 12-bit I2C DAC* Low cost (verify price)* Link to product * 12-bit resolution* Runs from 2.7 V to 5.5 V, compatible with the 5 V supply* Simple two-wire I2C interface* Built-in EEPROM remembers its last output setting * Costs more than the internal DAC* Needs an I2C driver and extra wiring* I2C speed limits how fast samples can be updated

Choice: Option 1: PIC18F57Q43 Internal 8-bit DAC

Rationale: The PIC18F57Q43's internal 8-bit DAC is the best fit for this project. We already own the microcontroller board, so using its built-in peripheral adds no cost and no shipping or lead-time risk. Eight bits is sufficient for speech-quality audio, and the on-chip DAC removes the need for an SPI or I2C driver and extra wiring, which keeps both the firmware and the board layout simple. The DAC7512 and MCP4725 would offer higher resolution (12-bit), but that improvement is not needed for voice, and either one would add cost, a custom driver, and delivery delays. The main tradeoff is a higher quantization noise floor, which is acceptable for this application.

Table 2: Microphone Component Selection

Microphone — Individual Subsystem

Solution Pros Cons * Option 1. * CUI Devices CMC-6027-24T Electret Microphone* Low cost (verify price)* Link to product * Low cost* Small 6 mm through-hole form factor* Analog output works directly with the PIC's ADC* Simple to prototype and solder* Can be biased from the 5 V supply * Output signal is very small and needs amplification* Needs a bias resistor and DC-blocking capacitor* Analog signal is susceptible to noise * Option 2. * Adafruit MAX9814 Microphone Amplifier Breakout* About $8/each (verify price)* Link to product * Built-in amplifier with automatic gain control* Higher output level, so less external circuitry* Ready to use on a breadboard * More expensive* Automatic gain control can distort or pump the audio* Hides the amplifier stage we are supposed to design * Option 3. * Knowles SPU0410LR5H-QB Analog MEMS Microphone* Moderate cost (verify price)* Link to product * Very small and consistent from part to part* Built-in preamplifier, so a larger output signal* Low noise and flat frequency response * Surface-mount only, which does not fit our through-hole PCB* Supply voltage is limited to about 3.6 V, below our 5 V rail* More expensive than an electret capsule

Choice: Option 1: CUI Devices CMC-6027-24T Electret Microphone

Rationale: The CMC-6027-24T is selected because it is inexpensive, small, and gives a plain analog signal that the PIC18F57Q43's ADC can read once it is amplified. It is a through-hole part, so it fits our PCB, and it can be biased directly from the 5 V rail. Its output is small, so it pairs with the MCP6004 amplifier stage in the next table, and the extra bias and coupling components are cheap and easy to add. The MAX9814 breakout is more convenient, but it costs more and its built-in gain stage would replace the amplifier circuit that this subsystem is meant to design. The MEMS microphone is compact and quiet, but it is surface-mount only and cannot run from our 5 V rail without extra circuitry. The main tradeoff of the electret is added circuit complexity and noise sensitivity, which we address with proper decoupling and filtering before the ADC input.

Table 3: Amplifier Component Selection

Operational Amplifier — Individual Subsystem

Solution Pros Cons * Option 1. * Microchip MCP6004 Quad Op Amp* Low cost (verify price)* Link to product * Rail-to-rail input and output* Runs from 1.8 V to 6 V, compatible with the 5 V supply* Low power consumption* Spare op amps available for buffering the half-supply reference * Gain-bandwidth of about 1 MHz limits very high gain* Four amplifiers in one package, so most go unused* Higher input noise than precision audio op amps * Option 2. * Texas Instruments LM358 Dual Op Amp* Low cost (verify price)* Link to product * Very common and easy to find* Through-hole DIP package is breadboard-friendly* Wide supply range * Output cannot swing to the positive rail, wasting part of the ADC range on a 5 V supply* Not rail-to-rail, so it handles a single-supply audio signal poorly* Higher power consumption * Option 3. * Texas Instruments TLV9001 Single Op Amp* Low cost (verify price)* Link to product * Rail-to-rail input and output* Runs from 1.8 V to 5.5 V, compatible with the 5 V supply* Low power consumption * Single amplifier, so there are no spares to buffer the half-supply reference* Only available in surface-mount packages, which does not fit our through-hole PCB* Gain-bandwidth of about 1 MHz limits very high gain

Choice: Option 1: Microchip MCP6004 Quad Op Amp

Rationale: The MCP6004 is selected because it runs from the same 5 V rail as the rest of the subsystem and has rail-to-rail input and output, so the amplified microphone signal can use the full 0 to 5 V range of the ADC around the 2.5 V half-supply reference. Its low power draw suits a small design, and the extra amplifiers in the package are used as buffers on the half-supply reference so they do not pick up noise. The LM358 is easier to find in a DIP package, but its output cannot reach the positive rail. The TLV9001 has similar electrical performance, but it is a single amplifier in a surface-mount package only. The tradeoff is a modest gain-bandwidth product, which is more than enough for speech frequencies.

Table 4: Voltage Regulator Component Selection

Voltage Regulator — Individual Subsystem

Solution Pros Cons * Option 1. * onsemi MC7805CTG 5 V Linear Regulator (TO-220)* Low cost (verify price)* Link to product * Fixed 5 V output with no adjustment needed* Accepts a 9 V wall adapter (input up to 35 V)* Delivers up to 1 A* Through-hole package fits our PCB* Built-in thermal overload and current limiting * Dropout of about 2 V, so it needs at least 7 V in* Wastes the voltage difference as heat* Bulkier than newer low-dropout parts * Option 2. * Texas Instruments TLV761 (5.0 V fixed-output version)* Low cost (verify price)* Link to product * Input voltage up to 18 V, so a 9 V adapter works* Delivers up to 1 A* Low dropout, about 0.9 V typical at 1 A* Low quiescent current, about 60 µA* ±1% output accuracy* Stable with a 1 µF ceramic output capacitor * Surface-mount only (SOT-223 or TO-252), which does not fit our through-hole PCB* The 5.0 V version must be ordered specifically* Harder to hand-solder than a TO-220 * Option 3. * LM2940-5.0 Low-Dropout 5 V Regulator* Moderate cost (verify price)* Link to product * Very low dropout, about 0.5 V* Delivers up to about 1 A* Wide input voltage range * More expensive* Requires an output capacitor of at least 22 µF with controlled ESR* More demanding to lay out

Choice: Option 1: onsemi MC7805CTG 5 V Linear Regulator

Rationale: The MC7805CTG is selected because the whole subsystem runs from a single 5 V rail, and the unregulated 9 V DC wall adapter plugs into a barrel jack and gives it plenty of headroom above the regulator's 2 V dropout. It is a through-hole TO-220 part, so it matches our PCB, and it needs only a small input and output capacitor. The subsystem draws well under 100 mA, so the heat wasted dropping 9 V to 5 V is small and no heat sink is needed. The TLV761 and LM2940 have lower dropout and better efficiency, but we do not need that with a 9 V source, and the TLV761 is surface-mount only, which does not fit our through-hole PCB. The tradeoff of the MC7805CTG is the wasted power as heat, which is acceptable at this current.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Starting with power: a 9 volt DC wall adapter plugs into a barrel jack (J1) and feeds an LM7805 5 volt regulator through a 1 amp fuse and a jumper (JP1) that lets me disconnect power. Capacitors on the regulator’s input and output, plus a 1k load resistor on the output, give a clean 5 volts. That 5 volts feeds the Nano’s VTG pin, with a 0.1 microfarad capacitor next to it, and the VBUS pin is left unconnected. Everything runs from this single 5 volt rail, including the PIC, the mic, and the op amp. Because the PIC’s supply is also 5 volts, the ADC range is 0 to 5 volts, so the op amp output can’t go above what RA0 can handle.

For the mic, a 2.2k resistor from 5 volts biases it. A 1 microfarad capacitor blocks DC and passes only the sound. Because I only have a single supply, I build a half-supply reference of about 2.5 volts, called VB, with two 10k resistors and a 10 microfarad capacitor. A 100k resistor ties the op amp input to VB.

The op amp is a non-inverting amplifier. A 47k feedback resistor and a 2.2k resistor in series with a 10 microfarad capacitor to ground give about 22 times gain on audio. DC passes at a gain of one, so the 2.5 volt center stays put. I wired the three unused amplifiers as buffers on VB, so they don’t pick up noise.

The output goes through a 4.7k resistor and a 10 nanofarad capacitor. That’s a low-pass filter at about 3.4 kilohertz, which protects RA0 and reduces aliasing at an 8 kilohertz sample rate.

The 8-pin header (J2) connects to Sultan’s system: RX on pin 1 (RA1), TX on pin 2 (RB2), and ground on pin 8, matching our block diagram. Pins 3 through 7 are not connected. A second header (J4) breaks out spare GPIO (RC6, RD4, RA3, RA4) with 5 volts and ground. The (un)mute button on RC4 pulls the pin to ground, and the debugging LED on RC5 has a 300 ohm resistor. I added test points for 5 volts, ground, VB, MIC_OUT and ADC_IN, put no-connect flags on every unused pin, and ran KiCad’s electrical rules check to catch mistakes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A power budget was created to determine the current requirements of the microphone subsystem and verify that the selected power source can safely support the complete circuit. The board uses a single 5 V power rail. A 9 V DC wall adapter feeds an onsemi MC7805CTG linear regulator, which produces the 5 V rail and powers the Curiosity Nano through its VTG pin. Current requirements were estimated for the MCP6004 operational amplifier, the CMC-6027-24T electret microphone, the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, and the red test LED. The DAC is the PIC18F57Q43’s internal 8-bit DAC, so it is part of the microcontroller and does not add a separate load.

The estimated maximum current consumption of these components is approximately 24.7 mA. A 25% safety margin was added to account for variations in component current consumption and operating conditions, resulting in a design requirement of approximately 30.9 mA on the 5 V rail. This value was compared with the 1000 mA rating of the MC7805CTG, and then the regulator’s input current (rail current plus its quiescent current) was compared with the rating of the 9 V wall adapter to verify that sufficient current capacity is available.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The completed power budget indicates that the microphone subsystem can operate from a single 5 V rail. After applying the 25% safety margin, the calculated maximum current requirement is approximately 30.9 mA. The MC7805CTG is rated for 1000 mA, leaving approximately 969 mA of capacity on the rail. The regulator draws about 37.4 mA from the 9 V wall adapter, which leaves more than 960 mA of capacity on the external source.

The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano and the red test LED represent the largest portions of the estimated current consumption, while the MCP6004 and the microphone draw very little. The 1 kΩ output load resistor and the half-supply voltage divider draw about 5 mA together, which is covered by the safety margin. The power budget demonstrates that the selected regulator and wall adapter provide adequate current capacity, although the actual current consumption should be measured during subsystem verification to confirm the design estimates.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The physical layout translates the verified schematic onto a dual-layer printed circuit board meticulously optimized for signal integrity, noise isolation, and manufacturing requirements. The entire design is constrained to a compact physical footprint under 100mm x 100mm, routed precisely on the Edge.Cuts layer.

docs.title: Design Rules and Routing Strategy
docs.text: To meet the stringent Peralta PCB mill specifications, trace widths and spacing rules were strictly applied across the entire layout: * Signal Traces: Configured with a standard trace width of 0.4mm and a clearance rule of 0.254mm to eliminate the risk of mill-bridge shorts. * Power Distribution: High-current traces (>500mA) along the primary 5V supply rail are routed at an expanded width of 0.8mm to 1.0mm to handle current demands safely and reduce trace impedance. * Ground Planes: Solid copper ground zones are poured across both the top (F.Cu) and bottom (B.Cu) layers, tied directly to the Earth/GND net. These continuous planes provide an excellent low-impedance return path for the high-frequency digital lines of the PIC microcontroller, suppressing switching transients and shielding the fragile analog audio signals.

docs.title: Component Placement and Signal Integrity
docs.text:
Components are arranged logically to separate noisy digital switching circuits from high-gain analog audio elements: * Analog Section: The electret microphone biasing network, the half-supply voltage reference (\(V_B\)), and the non-inverting op-amp circuitry are grouped closely together to keep high-impedance traces as short as possible, preventing noise pickup. * Digital Section: The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano module sits centralized to streamline routing to the off-board system headers. Unused op-amp pins are cleanly tied to buffers to prevent floating oscillations. * Manufacturing Details: To meet submission criteria, custom footprint pad mappings were fully matched with their schematic pin configurations. Large, bold initials (MD) are permanently etched directly into the copper on the top layer (F.Cu) for unmistakable board identification. Test points are left fully accessible to facilitate rapid probing of the 5V, GND, VB, MIC_OUT, and ADC_IN nodes.
